summary:
I've been building a career assistant that lives on this site and only answers from what's actually published here — it can't invent projects I haven't written down. It routes across a couple of model providers, and if the one it's talking to gets slow or busy, it falls back cleanly instead of the answer degrading.

Behind the scenes I run one shared GPU across everything that wants it — a chat model, an image generator, a couple of others — through a small proxy I call Switchboard. It queues requests and evicts whatever's resident so nothing collides. The more interesting piece was getting one of those models to serve two people at once instead of one after another: two simultaneous requests now finish in about the time a single one used to take, so I'm getting roughly double the throughput out of the same card without adding hardware.

BudgetTracker, my personal finance tracker, is deployed and live. I recently gave my own AI assistant read-only access to it through a set of tools that do their math in SQL rather than trusting the model to add up numbers itself, with account access scoped per key so nothing leaks across accounts it shouldn't see.

On the hardware side I've got a barbell rep counter running on a small ESP32 board — no machine learning, just onboard logic and a live dashboard — and a couch presence sensor that pauses the TV when I get up. That one went through a pivot: the camera-based version turned out to be unreliable, so I swapped it for a radar sensor instead.

highlights.oneLiner: Career assistant answers only from published site content, routes across providers, falls back cleanly under load
Shared-GPU proxy now serves one model to two users at once, ~2x throughput on the same card
Gave the personal AI assistant read-only, per-key-scoped access via SQL-side math tools
Pivoted from unreliable camera detection to a radar sensor for auto-pausing the TV
